args.summary:
This is the official National Bureau of Statistics of China (国家统计局) Statistical Communiqué on the 2023 National Economic and Social Development (中华人民共和国2023年国民经济和社会发展统计公报), published on February 29, 2024. It provides comprehensive annual economic and social statistics for China in 2023.

KEY ECONOMIC INDICATORS (综合):
- GDP reached 1,260,582 billion yuan (126.06 trillion yuan), up 5.2% year-on-year. Primary industry: 89,755 billion yuan (+4.1%); Secondary: 482,589 billion yuan (+4.7%); Tertiary: 688,238 billion yuan (+5.8%). Tertiary sector accounted for 54.6% of GDP.
- Per capita GDP: 89,358 yuan (+5.4%); GNI: 1,251,297 billion yuan (+5.6%).
- Quarterly GDP growth: Q1 +4.5%, Q2 +6.3%, Q3 +4.9%, Q4 +5.2%.
- Final consumption contributed 4.3 percentage points to GDP growth; capital formation 1.5 points; net exports dragged -0.6 points.

POPULATION:
- Year-end population: 1,409.67 million, a decrease of 2.08 million from prior year. Births: 9.02 million (6.39‰); deaths: 11.10 million (7.87‰); natural growth rate: -1.48‰ (population decline).
- Urban population: 932.67 million (66.2%); rural: 477.0 million. Male 51.1%, female 48.9%. 60+ population: 296.97 million (21.1% of total); 65+: 216.76 million (15.4%).
- Urbanization rate: 66.16% (+0.94 pct points).
- Employed persons: 740.41 million; urban new employment: 12.44 million (+380,000). Urban surveyed unemployment rate averaged 5.2%. Migrant workers: 297.53 million (+0.6%).

PRICES & FINANCE:
- CPI rose 0.2%; PPI fell 3.0%; producer purchase prices fell 3.6%.
- Foreign exchange reserves: $3,238 billion (+$110.3 billion). RMB average exchange rate: 7.0467 yuan/USD (depreciated 4.5%).
- M2: 292.3 trillion yuan (+9.7%); M1: 68.1 trillion (+1.3%). Social financing increment: 35.6 trillion yuan.
- General public budget revenue: 216,784 billion yuan (+6.4%); expenditure: 274,574 billion (+5.4%).

AGRICULTURE:
- Grain output: 695.41 million tons (+1.3%). Corn +4.2%, soybeans +2.8%; rice -0.9%, wheat -0.8%. Meat output: 96.41 million tons (+4.5%); pork +4.6%. Aquatic products: 71 million tons (+3.4%).

INDUSTRY:
- Total industrial value added: 399,103 billion yuan (+4.2%); above-scale industrial value added +4.6%. Automotive manufacturing +13.0%; electrical machinery +12.9%; chemicals +9.6%.
- NEV production: 9.443 million units (+30.3%); solar cells: 540 million kW (+54.0%); service robots: 7.833 million sets (+23.3%).
- Above-scale industrial enterprise profits: 76,858 billion yuan (-2.3%). Capacity utilization: 75.1%.
- Crude steel: 1,019.081 million tons (0.0%); steel: 1,362.682 million tons (+5.2%).

ENERGY:
- Primary energy output: 4.83 billion tons of standard coal (+4.2%). Coal output: 4.71 billion tons (+3.4%); crude oil: 209.026 million tons (+2.1%); natural gas: 232.43 billion cubic meters (+5.6%); electricity generation: 9,456.44 billion kWh (+6.9%).
- Installed power capacity: 2,919.65 million kW (+13.9%). Solar installed capacity +55.2%; wind +20.7%.
- Clean energy power generation: 3,190.6 billion kWh (+7.8%).

SERVICES:
- Retail/wholesale +6.2%; transport/warehousing/postal +8.0%; accommodation/catering +14.5%; finance +6.8%; real estate -1.3%; IT/software +11.9%.
- Freight volume: 55.7 billion tons (+8.1%); passenger transport: 9.3 billion person-trips (+66.5%).
- Civilian vehicle ownership: 336.18 million (+17.14 million); private cars: 186.68 million.
- Express delivery: 13.207 billion parcels; telecom business volume: 1,832.7 billion yuan (+16.8%). Mobile phone users: 1,726.6 million. Internet users: 1.092 billion; internet penetration: 77.5%. 5G base stations: 3.38 million.

DOMESTIC TRADE:
- Total retail sales of consumer goods: 471,495 billion yuan (+7.2%). Catering revenue: 52,890 billion (+20.4%). Online physical goods retail: 130,174 billion yuan (+8.4%), 27.6% of total retail.

FIXED ASSET INVESTMENT:
- Total: 509,708 billion yuan (+2.8%); excluding households: 503,036 billion (+3.0%). Infrastructure investment +5.9%. Manufacturing investment +6.5%. Real estate development investment: 110,913 billion yuan (-9.6%).
- New commercial housing sales: 1,117.35 million sqm (-8.5%). New housing starts: -20.4%. Housing completions: +17.0%.
- 1.59 million shantytown units started; 2.13 million affordable rental housing units; 53,700 old urban residential communities renovated.

FOREIGN TRADE:
- Total goods trade: 417,568 billion yuan (+0.2%); exports: 237,726 billion (+0.6%); imports: 179,842 billion (-0.3%); trade surplus: 57,883 billion yuan.
- Belt & Road countries: 194,719 billion yuan (+2.8%). Private enterprises: 53.5% of total trade.
- Automobile exports: 5.22 million units (+57.4%), value 7,165 billion yuan (+76.8%).
- Services trade: 65,754 billion yuan (+10.0%); deficit 12,041 billion yuan.
- FDI: 53,766 new enterprises (+39.7%); actual FDI use: 1,133.9 billion yuan (-8.0%), $163.3 billion (-13.7%). OFDI (non-financial): 917 billion yuan (+16.7%), $130.1 billion.

RESIDENT INCOME & CONSUMPTION:
- Per capita disposable income: 39,218 yuan (+6.3% nominal, +6.1% real). Urban: 51,821 yuan (+5.1%); rural: 21,691 yuan (+7.7%). Urban/rural income ratio: 2.39 (narrowed by 0.06).
- Per capita consumption expenditure: 26,796 yuan (+9.2% nominal, +9.0% real). Engel coefficient: 29.8%.
- Migrant worker average monthly income: 4,780 yuan (+3.6%). Poverty-alleviated counties rural per capita income: 16,396 yuan (+8.5%).

SOCIAL SECURITY:
- Urban employees' basic pension: 521.21 million participants; basic medical insurance: 1,333.87 million; unemployment insurance: 243.73 million; work injury insurance: 301.70 million.

S&T AND EDUCATION:
- R&D expenditure: 33,278 billion yuan (+8.1%), 2.64% of GDP. Invention patents granted: 921,000 (+15.3%). Valid invention patents: 4.991 million (+18.5%).
- 66 successful space launches; C919 commercial operation began; first domestic large cruise ship completed sea trials; space station entered application/development phase.
- Graduate enrollment: 1.302 million; undergraduate/vocational enrollment: 10.422 million; nine-year compulsory education consolidation rate: 95.7%.

CULTURE, TOURISM, HEALTH, SPORTS:
- Domestic tourist trips: 4.89 billion (+93.3%); total domestic tourism spending: 49,133 billion yuan (+140.3%). Inbound visitors: 82.03 million; outbound: 100.96 million.
- Medical institutions: 1.071 million; health technicians: 12.47 million; hospital beds: 10.2 million; total diagnoses: 9.56 billion.
- Sports venues: 4.593 million; per capita sports area: 2.89 sqm. Athletes won 165 world championships in 32 events; 201 gold medals at Hangzhou Asian Games (11th consecutive top ranking).

RESOURCES & ENVIRONMENT:
- Energy consumption: 5.72 billion tons of standard coal (+5.7%); coal 55.3% of energy mix (down 0.7 pct points); clean energy 26.4% (up 0.4 pct points). Energy intensity per unit GDP fell 0.5%.
- PM2.5 average: 30 μg/m³ (+3.4%). 59.9% of 339 cities met air quality standards. 89.4% of surface water sections rated excellent/good (I-III class).
- Production safety accidents: 21,242 deaths (-4.7%).

All data are preliminary figures and exclude Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan. Data sources include multiple government ministries and agencies.

時報看中國

# 調查顯示中國貧富失衡，中產階級自安現狀

儲百亮

![北京的辦公室員工。儘管收入增加，但研究指出，中國的貧富不均及教育和醫療等社會保障方面的機會不平等現象在加深。](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2016/01/28/world/28chinasociety/28chinasociety-master1050.jpg)

北京的辦公室員工。儘管收入增加，但研究指出，中國的貧富不均及教育和醫療等社會保障方面的機會不平等現象在加深。 Gilles Sabrie for The New York Times

北京——習近平將其稱為他的「中國夢」——一個有凝聚力的平等社會，日益富裕，健康狀況不斷改善，樂見共產黨的統治，熱切追求愛國主義和傳統價值觀。這一設想在這裡的電視和街頭廣告牌上隨處可見，為習近平的誓言助威。他宣稱：在他的治理下，中國社會將變得更加公正平等。

不過，北京的研究機構有兩項新研究表明，雖然中國民眾依然安於現狀——儘管並不總是十分滿意——但習近平卻面臨著不滿情緒帶來的一股持續暗流：收入、教育機會和醫療保健等領域的不平等。在經濟繼續疲軟的情況下，這種社會壓力可能會帶來麻煩。

[中國家庭追蹤調查(China Family Panel Studies)](http://www.isss.edu.cn/cfps/)的2015年度報告稱：「中國未來發展將面臨一系列嚴峻的挑戰。」該報告由北京大學中國社會科學調查中心撰寫。

「在我國整體財富迅速增長的同時，社會中存在的不均等現象也日益凸顯，」報告中寫道。「這不僅體現在收入與財富的兩極分化，在教育、健康等社會保障獲取層面上的差異也顯而易見。」

習近平和總理李克強一直表示，當務之急是克服這些社會不平衡。但這份報告提醒人們，還有更多的工作需要完成。報告根據一項年度調查的結果撰寫，涵蓋了逾3.5萬名成人和1.3萬個家庭。

「這些問題亟需得到有效解決，」文中提到。「否則很有可能威脅社會的穩定，進而成為未來社會經濟發展的瓶頸。」

這項研究引起了不少反響。有[新聞報道](http://thediplomat.com/2016/01/report-chinas-1-percent-owns-13-of-wealth/)引用它的結論：中國收入最高的1%家庭擁有全國三分之一的國內財富，而收入最低的四分之一家庭只有1%。其實這一發現已在去年的研究中體現了，而今年報告的重點是獲得住房、教育和醫療服務的機會。

研究表明，家庭背景在決定人的教育水平中起到巨大作用，特別是父母的教育程度，這是所有社會共有的。但在中國，政治特權也是重要因素。父親是否為共產黨員——政府官員幾乎必須是黨員——是你教育程度的一個決定性因素。研究發現，甚至對於在鄧小平以市場為本的政策下於1980年以後出生的中國人而言，情況也是如此。

「父親是黨員一直對個人受教育年限有顯著正向影響，」研究報告稱。（研究發現，母親是否擁有黨員身份沒有明顯影響。）

研究還發現，雖然對女生的歧視有所減弱，但這仍然是影響她們接受教育機會的重要因素。平均而言，男生上學年限比女孩多一年半。

對很多中國人來說，特別是農村和小城鎮居民，醫療機會不平等也一直是滋生不滿情緒的一個原因。這些地區的醫療保險覆蓋面較窄，醫生和醫院也較少。

這項調查發現，中國政府在擴展醫療保險方面的努力起到了一定作用。越來越多的農村居民享受到了一些醫保，但通常不及許多城市居民享有的政策優厚。而且，女性比男性獲益少。

「女性、農村居民和低收入群體享受到了更少的醫療補貼，他們的自付比例較高，」文中指出。

組成中國中產階級的專業人士、管理人員、白領員工和業主既承載了國家領導人的希望，也代表了他們的焦慮。如果這群人的規模、收入和滿意度增加，中產階級可以持續成為共產黨統治的穩定支柱。但是，倘若這群較為富裕的受過教育的城市階層變得不滿，那麼黨對權力的掌控便可能會削弱。

北京大學的研究說明，就目前而言，中國大多數中產階級似乎在大多數情況下安於現狀。就算考慮到很多中國人可能不願意批評政府，儘管是在調查里，也沒有依據表明較富裕的城市居民有意挑戰黨的統治。

研究發現，自認為屬於社會「中上層」的應答者當中，約60%對當地政府的表現持正面看法。相比之下，自認為屬於最底層級的人當中，這一數據則為48%。

「與工人階層特別是國有部門工人階層相比，我國中產階層的貧富差距感知、幹部信任水平和政府績效評價相對積極，」文中指出。「中產階層具有成為『社會穩定器』的潛質。」

但這也有可能發生變化。中國社會科學院發佈的覆蓋逾3000人的另一項調查發現，中國中產階級要比社會其他成員更積極地參與政治事務。

此項調查自2014年底開始進行了12個月，結果發表在社科院的2016年《社會藍皮書》上。調查發現，北京、上海和廣州的中產階級應答者當中，42.%的人表示，會與身邊人討論政治。只有27.7%的非中產階級成員做出同樣表示。

This is an opinion/commentary article by He Qinglian (何清涟), written for Voice of America (VOA), arguing that China's social transformation has failed, specifically regarding the transformation of its social class structure. The article contends that China has failed to transition from a pyramid-shaped society dominated by a large lower class to an olive-shaped society dominated by a middle class.

Key arguments and data points:

1. **Class Structure Transformation Failure**: He cites Chinese scholar Zi Zhongjun's (资中筠) remark that "in 100 years, nothing has progressed—above is still Cixi (Empress Dowager), below is still the Boxers," arguing this illustrates that China's class structure transformation has failed. The lower class remains too large while the middle class is too small as a percentage of the population.

2. **Middle Class Statistics**: In February 2010, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) "Contemporary Chinese Social Structure Change" research group concluded that China's middle class was about 23% of the total population, growing at roughly 1 percentage point per year. The article criticizes the Asian Development Bank's 2010 report that defined the middle class as those spending $2-20 per day, which counted 817 million Chinese as middle class (including 303 million "lower middle class" spending just $2/day), calling this "absurd" and noting many Chinese felt "counted as middle class" against their will.

3. **Poverty Statistics**: According to World Bank data, about 300 million Chinese live on $1 or less per day. Combined with ADB's 303 million "lower middle class," China's poor and semi-poor population approaches half the population (including 200 million unemployed cited by former Premier Wen Jiabao in March 2010). The article claims the social bottom stratum (poor and semi-poor) may exceed 60% of the population, and that an additional 124 million people could lose jobs due to foreign capital withdrawal and real economy downturn.

4. **Unfair Distribution System as Root Cause**: The article argues that the failure stems from unfair income distribution. Key problems include:

5. **Gini Coefficient**: China's "household net asset Gini coefficient" reached 0.73 in 2012 (per Peking University's China Social Survey Center's "China People's Livelihood Development Report 2014"). The top 1% of households hold over one-third of national property, while the bottom 25% hold only about 1%.

6. **Positive Factors Gone**: The article argues that conditions for middle class growth—increasing modern-sector employment and wage growth—have not materialized. Social mobility channels have become severely blocked. The "principle of bloodline" (family background inheritance) increasingly trumps achievement principles in elite selection, causing elite quality deterioration and worsening social injustice. He references her earlier BBC article (March 1, 2010) predicting these outcomes.

7. **Conclusion**: The article notes that in the Xu Chunhe incident (徐纯合事件), Chinese public opinion showed near-unanimous support for the deceased, reflecting not just hatred of public power abuse but deep class division ("tearing") in Chinese society.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an interview-based analysis of China's middle class (中产阶层), published September 21, 2012 on 社会学视野网 (Sociology Vision Net), authored by Lu Hanlong (卢汉龙), a researcher at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences (SASS) Institute of Sociology. The article combines a published paper and an interview with Lu conducted by the Oriental Morning Post/Shanghai Economic Review on July 20.

KEY POINTS:

1. **Defining China's Middle Class**: Lu argues the concept of "middle class" originated with Marx, referring to small/mid-sized entrepreneurs between capitalists and workers. It expanded to management in the late 19th/early 20th century, and by the 1960s (post-industrial era) included knowledge workers, white-collar professionals, and sometimes civil servants. Three groups qualify: (1) small/mid-capitalists and private entrepreneurs, (2) enterprise managers and professionals (engineers, doctors, judges), (3) civil servants.

2. **Statistics**: Asian Development Bank's 2010 report estimated China's middle class at 817 million people (by their standard); the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' "Contemporary Chinese Social Structure Change" project put the middle class at 23% of the population. By income/occupation, ~30% of urban Chinese qualify as middle class. In Shanghai, over half of locally-registered residents qualify by occupation.

3. **"被中产" (Being "middle-classed" against one's will)**: Lu argues China has "中产" (middle-income people) but NO "中产阶层" (middle class) because the latter requires subjective self-identification, which many Chinese middle-income earners lack. He advocates replacing "中产阶层" with "小康阶层" (moderately prosperous stratum) - a concept based on lifestyle and living standards rather than class, drawn from traditional Chinese thought contrasting with "大同" (Great Harmony).

4. **China vs. Western Middle Class**: Western middle classes developed alongside mature market institutions, human rights protections, and welfare systems. China's middle class lacks the political and social environment for corresponding behaviors. Private entrepreneurs face market access barriers, loan difficulties, and rising labor costs. China's income system is opaque, welfare/social security is fragmented (社保、镇保、综保、农保), and professionals (doctors, teachers, lawyers, judges) lack job security and must monetize their human capital, making these professions highly commercialized.

5. **Historical Context**: In 1930s Shanghai, white-collar workers were a significant group but operated under bureaucratic and semi-colonial capitalism without a complete civil society - they exhibited "小市民" (petty bourgeois) characteristics while being modern in orientation (rule-following, rational, admiring the West, pursuing perfection). After 1949 and through the pre-Cultural Revolution period, these groups retained influence and middle-class lifestyles despite asset nationalization in the mid-1950s.

6. **Middle Class Anxieties and Emigration**: Reasons for middle-class emigration include: talent drain (early overseas students rarely returned; even returnees aren't top-tier), weak research environments (especially natural sciences), ideological constraints on humanities/social sciences, better welfare systems abroad, unequal opportunities, environmental degradation, and food safety concerns. Future growth of the middle class is expected (especially white-collar workers), but welfare institutions are lacking. Foreign-enterprise white-collar workers face "glass ceilings" in promotion and pay gaps with expatriates, plus housing loans, education, and medical concerns.

7. **Recommendations to Alleviate Anxiety**: (1) Build robust welfare/social security systems, especially basic medical coverage; (2) strengthen job stability; (3) reduce income inequality and increase income transparency; (4) ensure educational equity (currently education has weak effects on intergenerational mobility; rural students have declining access to universities and elite universities).

8. **European Lessons**: After the 2008 financial crisis, Europe's middle class also became destabilized. The "Third Industrial Revolution" emphasizes creative/knowledge industries where production is combined with innovation. Lessons for China: give private enterprises space in retail and service sectors, abandon traditional industry classifications (secondary/tertiary boundaries are blurring), and emphasize "inclusive growth" - meaning (a) fair access to markets and opportunities and (b) shared benefits through social security. Welfare should be treated as a productive factor, not merely consumption. Social security design requires public discussion and perceived fairness across interest groups; fragmented identity-based schemes need supplementary funding channels to address historical inequities.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from People's Daily's "人民文摘" (People's Digest) examines the concept of the "Middle Income Trap" (中等收入陷阱) and how it relates to the personal financial anxieties of China's middle class ("中产阶层陷阱" or "中产陷阱"). 

The article opens with the viral anecdote of a Beijing white-collar worker earning 7,500 yuan/month who feels insecure, and the comments of CPPCC member Cui Yongyuan about earning over 10,000 yuan/month yet still feeling strapped for cash. These examples illustrate "middle class anxiety" (中产阶层焦虑).

**Definition of the Middle Income Trap:** A condition where a country's per-capita income reaches a middle level but fails to transform its economic development model, leading to stagnant growth. Countries typically break through the $1,000 GDP "poverty trap," accelerate through $1,000-$3,000, but stall around $3,000 per capita GDP. The World Bank's 2008 standards classed China as an "upper-middle-income country" with risk of falling into the trap. A joint report by former World Bank President Zoellick and China's Development Research Center warned China could become a "high-income country" by 2030, but only if it changes its development model and reflects on the government's role in economic management.

**Middle Class Standards in China (chronological):**
- 10 years before the article: CASS sociologist Zhang Wanli defined the "middle class" as individuals earning 2.5-3.5万元/year with car ownership and social/cultural consumption, roughly 15% of the employed population (~100 million people).
- 2005: National Bureau of Statistics defined middle-income urban households (avg. 3 members) as earning 60,000-500,000 yuan/year; projected middle class to grow from 5% of population in 2005 to 45% by 2020.
- 2006: "China New Consumer Special Report" defined lower-middle class as households earning 25,000-40,000 yuan/year, and upper-middle class as 40,000-100,000 yuan/year.
- 2011 CASS Blue Book: Based on Engel's coefficient, urban middle class per-capita disposable income was 16,200-37,300 yuan (households: 48,600-111,900 yuan); urban middle class reached 230 million people (~37% of urban population) in 2009.
- Statistically, the National Bureau of Statistics considers the middle-income stratum as those between the social average and median income. In 2011, urban per-capita disposable income was 21,810 yuan, with a median of 19,118 yuan. However, these statistical definitions don't match public perception of middle class status.

**Solutions:** The article argues that the national "Middle Income Trap" and individual "middle class trap" are two sides of the same coin. The state must enact reforms—narrowing wealth gaps, breaking monopolies, curbing housing price inflation, and strengthening the social security system—so the middle class can shed housing, education, medical, and pension burdens and dare to consume. In turn, a strong consuming middle class expands domestic demand, drives industrial upgrading, and reduces over-reliance on exports and investment, enabling sustainable growth. Individually, people should pursue career transformation, diversify income sources, plan investments scientifically, and adjust their mentality by reducing material desires and comparisons to pursue spiritual wealth for a happier life.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: [PDF] 中国中产阶级的增长及其现状 ---
URL: http://www.sociology2010.cass.cn/webpic/web/sociology/upload/2010/11/d20101126150642765.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an academic paper by Li Chunling (李春玲) of the Institute of Sociology, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, published in 《江苏社会科学》 (Jiangsu Social Sciences) 2008 No. 5, analyzing the growth and current status of China's middle class. The paper examines four aspects: (1) the size and growth rate of the middle class, (2) income and consumption, and (3) socio-political attitudes, using multiple data sources including national census data (1982, 1990, 2000), 1% population sampling (2005), CASS urban household income surveys (1988, 1995, 2002), CGSS national surveys (2001, 2006), and a Beijing middle-class survey (2007).

KEY FINDINGS ON SIZE AND GROWTH:
- Different definitions and indicators produce widely varying estimates of the middle class share: from 3.1% to 25% nationally, and 8% to 48.5% in urban areas. The most rigorous estimates suggest 4-5% nationally, ~10% in cities, and 12-15% in large cities.
- Using the EAMC (East Asian Middle Class) classification framework (developed by Hsin-Huang Michael Hsiao and Alvin Y. So, based on Goldthorpe's class schema), the paper estimates urban middle class growth from 1982-2006. The new middle class (professionals and managers) grew from 13.9% (1982) to ~18.8-23.6% of the urban population aged 16-60. The old middle class (small employers/self-employed) grew from nearly zero to about 10-20%. The broad middle class (new + old + marginal) constitutes roughly 60% of urban population (55% excluding elites), while the core middle class (new middle class only) is about 20-23% (15-18% excluding elites). Nationally, the broad middle class is ~27% and core middle class ~8-9%.
- Using income standards (2.5x urban per-capita income as threshold), the income middle class grew from 0.5% of urban population in 1988 to 8.6% of urban/town population in 2006 (4.6% nationally), with acceleration since 2001 (~1 percentage point growth per year).

INCOME AND CONSUMPTION:
- Income gap between new middle class and working class widened: from 1.3x in 1988 to 1.5x (1995), 1.7x (2002), and 2.3x (2006). The new middle class's income surpassed the old middle class and it emerged as a distinct high-income group by the 1990s.
- Home ownership: private housing ownership among urban population rose from 13.7% (1988) to 41.7% (1995) and 75.9% (2000). The new middle class reached 80.6% private home ownership. However, since 2006, soaring real estate prices have made housing a core "middle class anxiety" issue, especially for young white-collar workers.
- Car ownership remains low nationally (2.5% of households in 2006), but is concentrated among middle classes. From 2001-2006, new middle class car ownership rose to 7.0%, old middle class to 6.1%, and marginal middle class to 6.7%, with entrepreneurs at 100%.

SOCIO-POLITICAL ATTITUDES:
- The new middle class reports the most positive life satisfaction and future expectations (70.9% said their living standards improved over past 5 years; 68.6% expect improvement in next 5 years).
- On trust in government and evaluation of the current situation, the new middle class does not differ significantly from other classes—all show relatively high trust (94.1% trust the central government) and positive evaluations.
- On "state authority consciousness," the new middle class shows the weakest identification with authoritarian statements and the strongest democratic awareness among all classes. For example, only 20.5% agreed that "citizens need not concern themselves with national affairs," and only 48.2% agreed that "democracy means government acting for the people" (vs. 66-71% for other classes).
- The new middle class exhibits the strongest sense of group interest conflict (84.8% perceive conflicts between social groups; 58.1% expect conflicts to intensify). This is linked to rising "populist" sentiment, though the new middle class is internally split—the upper segment aligns with capitalists, while the lower-middle segment and marginal middle class sympathize with workers/poor.
- Despite democratic tendencies, the new middle class largely rejects immediate adoption of Western democracy (viewing it as unsuitable for China's current development stage), supports the existing system, and serves as a stabilizing force. However, internal divisions between the upper and lower segments of the new middle class could intensify social conflicts.

CONCLUSION:
- The middle class is undeniably growing in China, but remains a minority in the total population; China's social structure is still dominated by peasants and workers.
- The new middle class holds mixed socio-political attitudes—both supportive of the existing system (benefiting from economic growth) and possessing stronger democratic awareness and critical views of specific government policies (housing, healthcare, education, income redistribution). Their criticisms target specific policies, not the political system itself, and they generally maintain a mutually beneficial relationship with the government.
- Internal fragmentation of the new middle class (upper vs. lower-middle segments) could disrupt this balance and potentially exacerbate social conflicts.
</summary>

4. **Overall Structural Change**: Tsinghua professor Li Qiang's research shows China's social structure has shifted from "inverted T-shaped" to "土-shaped" (earth-shaped), with the middle class rising to 26-28% of the population (~300 million people). Urbanization rate reversed from 62.3% rural population in 2001 to 63.89% urban population in 2023. Education returns: bachelor's degree holders earn 73% more than high school graduates; 985-university rural enrollment dropped from 32% in 2010 to 19% in 2024. Professional job ratios between megacities and small cities differ by 3:1.

5. **Policy Paths**: The State Council's implementation opinions target raising middle-class proportion to 35%+ by 2035. Gini coefficient at 0.468 exceeds the international warning line. Key reforms needed: property and capital gains taxes, unified national social security, and pension "dual-track system" reform (three-tier city public institution retirees receive 6,800 yuan/month vs. enterprise workers' 3,200 yuan/month — a 2.1x gap). Youth dynamics: Gen Z "frugal luxury" (73% accept installment consumption), county-town entrepreneurship, and declining overseas graduate returns (US four-year degree costs 2.8 million yuan with 8,000 yuan/month starting salary, over 30-year payback period).

The article concludes China is undergoing deep social transformation, needing both individual rational decisions and systemic institutional innovation to transition from a "土-shaped" to an "olive-shaped" society. The comments section contains criticism questioning the data sources, with several commenters suggesting the report appears AI-generated and noting the report cannot be found elsewhere online.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
瑞信研究院（Credit Suisse Research Institute，简称CSRI）是瑞士瑞信集团（Credit Suisse）下属的专业研究机构及内部智库。研究院长期致力于全球财富领域研究，每年发布的《全球财富报告》是综合性的全球家庭财富分析报告，具有广泛影响力。近年来其研究范围已拓展至性别平等、可持续发展（ESG）、消费者行为等新兴议题。

【主要研究报告】
- 《全球财富报告》：标志性年度出版物。2018年报告指出中国总财富21世纪增长1300%达51.9万亿美元；2019年报告显示全球财富总值360万亿美元，中国家庭财富全球第二，百万富翁440万；2021年第十三份报告显示全球财富总额463.6万亿美元，成人人均财富87,489美元，中国财富总额85.1万亿美元，百万富翁620万（占全球10%），预计2026年达1220万；2023年第十四份报告（覆盖2022年）显示全球私人净财富减少11.3万亿美元至454.4万亿美元，成人人均财富84,718美元。
- 《CS Gender 3000》：2019年报告指出全球董事会女性成员占比十年内翻倍至20.6%，性别多元化程度更高的公司股价表现更佳。
- ESG领域：2021年《全球粮食体系：探索可持续发展解决方案》报告分析粮食浪费问题。
- 《新兴市场消费者调查报告》：2021年第十期揭示数字经济增长、健康生活方式和非必需品需求三大消费驱动主题。
- 《瑞信家族企业1000》：指出家族企业在疫情期间展现更强韧性，ESG表现更佳。
- 《全球投资回报年鉴》：与伦敦商学院联合出版，2022年版侧重讨论通胀、加息和分散投资。

【研究领域与关注重点】
核心为全球及区域财富分配、增长趋势、家庭资产结构及超高净值人群动态。中国在2011年总财富超越日本，2014年百万富翁数量超越日本，稳居全球财富第二。2022年针对全球年轻消费者调查显示，中国年轻消费者可持续发展参与度全球排名第三（仅次于墨西哥和印度），超过60%的中国年轻消费者愿意转向可持续交通和度假方式；年轻消费群体（16-40岁）占全球消费支出48%，预计2040年将升至69%。

【机构人员与观点】
- 瑞信董事长及瑞信研究院负责人雷安泽（Axel Lehmann）负责发布《全球财富报告》。
- 报告基于Anthony Shorrocks、James Davies、Rodrigo Lluberas和Daniel Waldenström教授等顶尖学者见解。
- Anthony Shorrocks指出2022年财富下滑主因是高通胀加美元升值，若汇率维持2021年水平，2022年全球财富将增加3.4%。
- Nannette Hechler-Fayd'herbe预测未来五年全球财富将增长38%，到2027年总额达629万亿美元，百万富豪将达8600万。
- 瑞信全球ESG与主题研究主管Eugène Klerk关注年轻一代气候问题及家族企业优势。

【历史沿革】
- 2015年：发布第六份报告，中国中产阶级财富7.34万亿美元，仅次于美日。
- 2016年：报告指出中国超高净值人士数量自2000年增加100倍。
- 2018年10月：中国财富增长1300%达51.9万亿美元。
- 2019年10月：第十份报告，中国家庭财富全球第二。
- 2020年：发布CS Gender 3000及家族企业报告。
- 2021年：第十三份报告，中国财富总额85.1万亿美元，较上年增长15.1%。
- 2022年2月：发布年轻消费者可持续发展报告；同年发布2022全球投资回报年鉴。
- 2023年：瑞信集团被瑞银集团收购后，双方联合发布第十四份《全球财富报告》。
</summary>

"高通胀加上美元兑多个货币升值是导致2022年财富下滑的主要原因。如果汇率仍维持在2021年的水平，2022年全球财富总额将增加3.4%，成年人口人均财富将增加2.2%。但即便以固定汇率计算，去年仍然是2008年以来财富增长最慢的一年。" —— Anthony Shorrocks", "未来五年，我们预计全球财富将增长38%，到2027年，总额将达到629万亿美元，成年人口人均财富预计将增长30%，达到110,270美元。此外，我们预计，未来五年百万富豪数量将显著增加，人数将达到8,600万，超高净值人士数量将达到37.2万。" —— Nannette Hechler-Fayd'herbe", "行为方式的改变还需要新技术的加持。仅调整饮食结构本身并不足以使粮食体系实现全方位的可持续发展。" —— Eugène Klerk", "最新一期家族企业报告进一步印证了我们此前研究所显示的家族企业相对非家族企业的诸多优势。...发现基于较低杠杆率和出色现金流生成能力的较为保守的传统财务模型是家族企业的一项宝贵财富。" —— Eugène Klerk", "2021年全球财富总额达463.6万亿美元，成人人均财富87,489美元，增长显著；其中中国财富总额为85.1万亿美元，百万富翁数量达620万，预计到2026年将达1220万。"

This is a news article from 36kr (published September 22, 2022) reporting on the Credit Suisse (瑞士信贷) annual Global Wealth Report (《全球财富报告》). The report covers global personal wealth data through 2021, highlighting record-breaking growth and notable developments in China's wealth landscape.

Key findings from the report:
- Global personal wealth totaled $463.6 trillion at the end of 2021, growing 9.8% year-over-year (12.7% in local currency terms, the fastest annual growth on record). Global per-capita wealth reached $87,489.
- China's total private wealth grew 15.1% to $85.1 trillion, with adult per-capita wealth rising 14.5% to $76,000. The US grew 15.5% to $158.2 trillion, with adult per-capita wealth at $560,800.
- During the first two years of the COVID-19 pandemic (Jan 2020 - Dec 2021), the number of ultra-high-net-worth (UHNW) individuals (net assets over $50 million) grew by nearly 90,000 people (over 50%), reaching 264,200 globally by end of 2021.
- The US leads globally in UHNW individuals with 141,100 (53% of global total), followed by China with 32,700 (12%), Germany (9,720), Canada (5,510), and India (4,980). Regionally, North America holds 56% of UHNW individuals.
- Global millionaires reached 62.5 million by end of 2021 (up 5.2 million). The US has 24.5 million millionaires (39.2% of global total), while China has 6.2 million (10%), followed by Japan (5.4%), UK (4.6%), and France (4.5%).
- Wealth inequality worsened: the top 1% (millionaires) held 47.8% of global wealth (up from 43.9% in 2019), while the bottom 53.2% of low-income individuals (wealth under $10,000) held only 1.1% of global wealth. Credit Suisse attributed this to strong growth in financial assets.
- The global middle-asset segment (wealth between $10,000-$100,000) grew from 504 million people in 2000 to 1.8 billion by end of 2021, reflecting rising prosperity in emerging economies, especially China.
- Credit Suisse projects some reversal in wealth growth for 2022/2023 due to global economic headwinds, but expects global wealth to grow by $169 trillion (36%) cumulatively by 2026, with middle-income countries as the main driver. Global per-adult wealth is expected to surpass $100,000 by 2024, and millionaires are projected to exceed 87 million by 2026 (up ~39%).
- The report forecasts that by 2026, China's millionaire count and UHNW individual count will both double, reaching 12.2 million and nearly 60,000 respectively.

The article was originally published on the WeChat public account "财联社" (Cailian Press) by author 刘蕊 (Liu Rui), and republished by 36kr with authorization. The article also includes reader comments discussing wealth inequality concerns in China.

URL: https://www.rmlt.com.cn/2025/0314/725400.shtml

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in 《国家治理》杂志 (National Governance magazine) 2025 Issue No. 5 by 人民智库 (People's Think Tank), argues that China has complete confidence and capability to cross the "middle-income trap." Published on March 14, 2025, the article examines both international case studies and Chinese practice.

Key points:
- In 2010, China entered the upper-middle-income economy category, while its economy shifted from high-speed to medium-high-speed growth, sparking debate about whether China can cross the "middle-income trap."
- The article cites Xi Jinping: "For China, the 'middle-income trap' must be crossed; the key is when to cross it and how to develop better after crossing. We have confidence in finding a balance between reform, development and stability, and between stable growth, structural adjustment, benefiting people's livelihoods, and promoting reform."
- Since the 18th Party Congress, China has steadily improved scientific and technological innovation capabilities, optimized industrial structure, improved people's quality of life, and accelerated green development.

**Countries that fell into the middle-income trap:**
- **Brazil**: GDP growth exceeded 10% annually in the 1960s-70s but stagnated after the 1980s. Problems included over-reliance on foreign capital and technology, insufficient innovation in domestic enterprises, high debt (central government debt reached 79.1% of GDP in 2022), severe income inequality (Gini coefficient 0.6 in 1995, 0.5 in 2022), and over-urbanization with poor public services.
- **Malaysia**: Growth slowed after the 1997 financial crisis. Problems included over-reliance on foreign investment, weakening competitiveness of labor-intensive products, ethnic conflicts and rigid systems (1970 "New Economic Policy" led to reduced Chinese private investment), and insufficient R&D spending (R&D as share of GDP was only 0.5% in 2000, 1.0% in 2010, 1.3% in 2015).

**Countries that successfully crossed to high-income status:**
- **Japan**: Successful industrial structure transformation (from labor-intensive to heavy industry in the 1940s-50s, to automotive and precision machinery in the 60s-70s, to technology-intensive sectors after the 1980s). Technology development followed the path of introduction-imitation-independent innovation. Implemented the "National Income Doubling Plan" in 1960, which increased wages by 0.65 times by 1970 and expanded the middle class. Addressed environmental pollution through the Environmental Agency, Environmental Basic Law, and promotion of energy-saving industries.
- **South Korea**: Entered middle-income status in the 1980s and crossed to high-income status in 2002 per World Bank standards. Transformed from "trade-based nation" to "technology-based nation." Progressed from labor-intensive light industries (1960s) to capital-intensive heavy industries (1970s) to knowledge/technology-intensive industries (1980s-90s). Technology followed the introduction-imitation-innovation path. Improved income distribution (Gini coefficient fell from 0.39 in 1980 to 0.26 in 1991, remaining below the 0.4 warning line).

**Summary of transformation lessons:**
1. **Industrial structure transformation and upgrading** is essential - countries must shift from labor/resource-intensive and capital-intensive industries to knowledge/technology-intensive industries. Data from 1990-2023 shows high-income countries (Japan, South Korea) have higher service industry shares and lower agricultural shares than middle-income countries (Brazil, Malaysia).
2. **Technological innovation** drives economic and social development transformation - successful countries emphasized digestion, absorption, and re-innovation of imported technology, achieving higher R&D spending ratios compared to middle-income countries that maintained low and slowly growing R&D investment.

The article concludes that China's unique path of modernization, characterized by rising innovation capability, optimized industrial structure, improved living standards, and green development, has laid a solid foundation for crossing the middle-income trap and becoming a high-income country, contributing Chinese wisdom to the modernization of developing countries.
</summary>

URL: https://www.bain.cn/news_info.php?id=2102

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the Bain & Company China site article (dated January 29, 2026) announcing the release of the "2025 China Personal Luxury Report." The report covers the state of China's personal luxury goods market in 2025 and provides an outlook for 2026.

Key findings from the report include:

- **Overall market performance**: The Chinese mainland personal luxury goods market contracted by 3%–5% in 2025, a significant moderation compared to the sharp decline in 2024. Early signs of recovery emerged in the third quarter, supported by favorable base effects and a more stable stock market.
- **Category performance (uneven)**:
  - Beauty & personal care: Best performer, returning to 4%–7% growth, driven by demand for ultra-premium skincare and fragrances.
  - Fashion: Declined 5%–8%.
  - Leather goods: Declined 8%–11% due to past/ongoing price increases and limited innovation.
  - Watches: Under severe pressure, declining 14%–17%, as consumers turned to other investment assets, secondhand alternatives, and smart devices.
  - Jewelry: Improved, with decline narrowing to 0%–5%, supported by value-preservation and rising gold prices.
- **Consumption repatriation**: 65% of Chinese luxury consumption occurred in the mainland (35% overseas), reflecting increased repatriation due to narrowed price gaps with Europe and Japan, visa-free policies, flexible tax refunds, and improved in-store experiences.
- **Daigou activity**: Slowed to 3% growth (from 5% in 2024) among the top 45 tracked brands, as brands tightened control over gray-market sales.
- **Secondhand luxury market**: Grew 15%–20% in 2025 but remains underpenetrated at less than 10% of the primary market (vs. 20%–30% in developed markets). Growth driven by increased supply, younger price-sensitive buyers, and livestreaming platforms.
- **Local Chinese luxury brands**: Gaining share through culturally relevant product design, digital-first "China-first" customer strategies, and competitive pricing enabled by local supply chains.
- **Consumer behavior**: Consumers became more selective, prioritizing value-driven items balancing quality, exclusivity, and practicality. VIC (high-value customers) remain the core driver, while younger aspiring consumers are delaying entry into the luxury market. Experience-based consumption (travel, wellness) continued to be favored.
- **2026 Outlook**: Bain expects modest growth in 2026, with a growing middle class, improving confidence, and favorable policies expected to direct more luxury consumption back to the mainland, though growth remains highly category- and brand-dependent.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"在经历了2024年的动荡后，2025年的市场开始稳定下来。虽然消费者信心仍有待提升，但我们已经看到市场重新调整的积极信号，尤其是下半年出现了复苏的初步迹象。此次回暖呈现出更为清晰的结构性特征：VIC（高价值客户）群体依然是奢侈品市场的核心驱动力，而年轻的潜力消费群体在进入奢侈品市场方面则呈现出更为谨慎、延后的节奏。" — Bruno Lannes, Senior Partner at Bain & Company

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**Bain & Company and Altagamma Release the 2025 Global Luxury Goods Market Study (November 25, 2025)**

The Bain-Altagamma annual Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study reveals that global luxury spending in 2025 will remain broadly stable at approximately €1.44 trillion, holding steady despite economic and geopolitical uncertainties. The market is undergoing significant structural shifts as consumers increasingly prioritize experiences over material possessions, moving away from "conspicuous consumption" toward "experiential indulgence" (wellness, connection, and self-reward).

**Key Market Data:**
- Global luxury spending: ~€1.44 trillion in 2025, flat versus 2024 (within ±1% at constant exchange rates)
- Personal luxury goods market: €358B in 2025 (vs. €369B in 2023, €364B in 2024), down ~2% at current exchange rates, flat at constant rates — indicating market maturity
- Consumer base has contracted from 400 million in 2022 to ~340 million in 2025
- New customer acquisition declined 5% between 2024-2025
- Active luxury shoppers fell from ~60% of addressable base (2022) to 40-45% (2025)
- "Big spenders" market share: 30% (€88B in 2019) → 45% (€165B in 2024) → stabilizing at 46-47% (€165B in 2025)
- EBIT margins for personal luxury brands: peaked at 23% in 2012, expected to hit 15-16% in 2025 (back to 2009 levels)
- Margin contraction caused ~€100 billion loss in industry enterprise value over past 12 months
- High-end tier (40% of market) contracted with CAGR of -1% to -3% (2023-2025); accessible segment flat to slightly negative (0% to -2% CAGR)

**Segment Performance (2025):**
- Jewelry leads growth: +4-6% (driven by resilient demand, emotional appeal, customizable designs)
- Eyewear: +2-4% (design innovation, versatility, digital integration)
- Beauty stable; fragrances most dynamic sub-category; AI-driven personalization emerging
- Watches: polarized — high-end strong, tariffs/pricing pressure fueling resale market
- Apparel steady; leather goods wobble (lack of hero bags); shoes lag (price sensitivity, sportswear competition)
- Outlet stores outperforming in physical retail; online channels steady; monobrand store surface reduced by 25,000 sqm in six months; US department stores cut ~10% of space since 2024

**Regional Performance (2025):**
- China: expected to contract 3-5% (constant FX), pivoting to local accessible brands and experiences
- Japan: decelerating after strong 2024 due to cooling tourism
- Europe: down 1-3% (strong euro, geopolitical tensions, reduced tourist inflows)
- Americas: 0-2% growth (US domestic demand, Mexico and Brazil expansion)
- Middle East: strongest performer at 4-6% growth (Dubai, Abu Dhabi tourism; Saudi Arabia demand)
- Middle East, Latin America, Southeast Asia, India, and Africa combined: ~€45 billion in 2025, matching Chinese mainland scale

**Future Outlook:**
- Personal luxury goods projected to grow 4-6% annually through next decade
- By 2035: personal luxury goods market expected to reach €525-625B; overall luxury spending could reach €2.2-2.7 trillion

**Bruno Lannes (Senior Partner at Bain & Company)** emphasized that luxury brands face a critical moment: they must re-engage aspirational consumers, legitimize expansion into adjacent categories (food, dining, wellness), evolve from broad reach to precision, and rebuild trust through ethics, inclusivity, and authenticity. He noted the market is at a "crossroads" where brands must choose between embracing moral responsibility or retreating into traditional elitism.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"After the shopping spree era, experiences and emotions have become the true engine of luxury growth. The market remains resilient but not immune to macro-economic complexities, navigating a fragile global balance. Ahead lies a phase of quality-driven growth, fueled by discipline, ethics and innovation. Expansion will favor fewer, higher-impact locations—a shift toward a more discerning, experience-led model." — Bruno Lannes, Senior Partner, Bain & Company
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Bain & Company 2026 Global Luxury Market Study (Spring Update)

This webpage is a Chinese-language press release (dated 2026-07-14) from Bain & Company (贝恩公司) announcing the spring update of the 2026 Global Luxury Market Study, published in partnership with Altagamma, the Italian luxury goods manufacturers' industry association. The article covers key market data, regional performance, consumer behavior shifts, and strategic imperatives for luxury brands.

### Key Findings and Data:

**Overall Market:**
- Global luxury spending reached €1,443 billion in 2025, with the market gradually stabilizing in 2026.
- 2026 global luxury spending is projected at €1,440–1,470 billion (0–2% growth at constant exchange rates).
- Experiential luxury consumption is growing 1.5x faster than tangible goods in 2026, reflecting a shift from "owning luxury" to "experiencing the moment."

**Personal Luxury Goods Market:**
- 2025 sales dipped to €358 billion (from €364 billion in 2024; down 2% at current rates, up 1% at constant exchange rates).
- 2026 forecast: growth of 2–4% to €365–373 billion under the base case scenario (70% probability).
- Optimistic scenario: 4–6% growth (~20% probability); Conservative scenario: 0–2% growth (~10% probability).
- Q1 2026 was weak (down 3–5% at current rates), with Q2 showing signs of improvement. ~60% of luxury players outperformed their Q1 2025 results, and the brand performance gap narrowed.

**Regional Performance (Three Speeds):**
- **US/Americas:** Surging; US-native brands grew 10–15% YoY in Q1. Consumers under 35 spend ~4 percentage points faster than older cohorts. Upper middle-class households growing luxury spending at roughly twice the rate of wealthier cohorts.
- **China:** Cautious recovery; online luxury sales jumped 25–35% YoY in Q1. Ready-to-wear growing at twice the rate of leather goods as consumers shift from status purchases toward self-expression. Japan faces slowdown in tourist traffic, particularly from China.
- **Europe/Middle East:** Weak link; international tourist spending dropped ~20% in February. Gulf luxury consumer base shrank 15–25% in early 2026. Q2 shows tentative recovery signals (May tax refund data).

**Category Performance:**
- Jewelry leading; apparel, eyewear, and fragrances performing well.
- Cosmetics lagging; leather goods and footwear under pressure but improving.
- Watches: connoisseurship replacing hype, with resale market growing.
- Vintage bag searches more than doubled YoY; ~half of luxury shoppers check secondhand market before buying new.

**Macro Context:**
- Middle East conflict pushed oil prices up; US inflation at highest since April 2023; consumer confidence at all-time low.
- ECB raised interest rates in June (first since 2023); global GDP growth forecast weaker than 2025.
- Luxury share prices fell ~8% in January; European international tourism down 20% YoY in February.

**AI Impact:**
- ~Half of luxury consumers use AI in their purchase journey; nearly all plan to continue.
- One in four use AI for brand/product discovery; two in three use it for product comparison.
- Brands failing to build AI-native relevance risk being left behind.

**Other Notable Trends:**
- Sports sponsorship: over 80% of luxury market value comes from brands that sponsored sports in the past 12 months (mainly for brand-building, not direct sales).
- Immersive experiential bookings (dining, leisure, entertainment) up 30% YoY; travel beyond traditional hotspots up 20% (the "Elsewhereism" trend); ~50% of Gen-Z say brand preferences shaped by parents.
- Over 70% of customers who stopped buying luxury intend to return, but not necessarily to the same brands.

**Strategic Imperatives for Brands (Bain's Three Recommendations):**
1. Deliver wonder through immersive experiences in longevity escapes and untamed sanctuaries.
2. Build cultural relevance for diverse communities.
3. Offer clients a platform to co-author through AI-enabled creativity and personalization.

The report concludes that luxury's meaning is evolving from social validation ("status symbol") toward "self-actualization" and "living well," with consumer relationships shifting from product ownership to brand meaning.

# 調查顯示中國貧富失衡，中產階級自安現狀

儲百亮

![北京的辦公室員工。儘管收入增加，但研究指出，中國的貧富不均及教育和醫療等社會保障方面的機會不平等現象在加深。](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2016/01/28/world/28chinasociety/28chinasociety-master1050.jpg)

北京的辦公室員工。儘管收入增加，但研究指出，中國的貧富不均及教育和醫療等社會保障方面的機會不平等現象在加深。 Gilles Sabrie for The New York Times

北京——習近平將其稱為他的「中國夢」——一個有凝聚力的平等社會，日益富裕，健康狀況不斷改善，樂見共產黨的統治，熱切追求愛國主義和傳統價值觀。這一設想在這裡的電視和街頭廣告牌上隨處可見，為習近平的誓言助威。他宣稱：在他的治理下，中國社會將變得更加公正平等。

不過，北京的研究機構有兩項新研究表明，雖然中國民眾依然安於現狀——儘管並不總是十分滿意——但習近平卻面臨著不滿情緒帶來的一股持續暗流：收入、教育機會和醫療保健等領域的不平等。在經濟繼續疲軟的情況下，這種社會壓力可能會帶來麻煩。

[中國家庭追蹤調查(China Family Panel Studies)](http://www.isss.edu.cn/cfps/)的2015年度報告稱：「中國未來發展將面臨一系列嚴峻的挑戰。」該報告由北京大學中國社會科學調查中心撰寫。

「在我國整體財富迅速增長的同時，社會中存在的不均等現象也日益凸顯，」報告中寫道。「這不僅體現在收入與財富的兩極分化，在教育、健康等社會保障獲取層面上的差異也顯而易見。」

習近平和總理李克強一直表示，當務之急是克服這些社會不平衡。但這份報告提醒人們，還有更多的工作需要完成。報告根據一項年度調查的結果撰寫，涵蓋了逾3.5萬名成人和1.3萬個家庭。

「這些問題亟需得到有效解決，」文中提到。「否則很有可能威脅社會的穩定，進而成為未來社會經濟發展的瓶頸。」

這項研究引起了不少反響。有[新聞報道](http://thediplomat.com/2016/01/report-chinas-1-percent-owns-13-of-wealth/)引用它的結論：中國收入最高的1%家庭擁有全國三分之一的國內財富，而收入最低的四分之一家庭只有1%。其實這一發現已在去年的研究中體現了，而今年報告的重點是獲得住房、教育和醫療服務的機會。

研究表明，家庭背景在決定人的教育水平中起到巨大作用，特別是父母的教育程度，這是所有社會共有的。但在中國，政治特權也是重要因素。父親是否為共產黨員——政府官員幾乎必須是黨員——是你教育程度的一個決定性因素。研究發現，甚至對於在鄧小平以市場為本的政策下於1980年以後出生的中國人而言，情況也是如此。

「父親是黨員一直對個人受教育年限有顯著正向影響，」研究報告稱。（研究發現，母親是否擁有黨員身份沒有明顯影響。）

研究還發現，雖然對女生的歧視有所減弱，但這仍然是影響她們接受教育機會的重要因素。平均而言，男生上學年限比女孩多一年半。

對很多中國人來說，特別是農村和小城鎮居民，醫療機會不平等也一直是滋生不滿情緒的一個原因。這些地區的醫療保險覆蓋面較窄，醫生和醫院也較少。

這項調查發現，中國政府在擴展醫療保險方面的努力起到了一定作用。越來越多的農村居民享受到了一些醫保，但通常不及許多城市居民享有的政策優厚。而且，女性比男性獲益少。

「女性、農村居民和低收入群體享受到了更少的醫療補貼，他們的自付比例較高，」文中指出。

組成中國中產階級的專業人士、管理人員、白領員工和業主既承載了國家領導人的希望，也代表了他們的焦慮。如果這群人的規模、收入和滿意度增加，中產階級可以持續成為共產黨統治的穩定支柱。但是，倘若這群較為富裕的受過教育的城市階層變得不滿，那麼黨對權力的掌控便可能會削弱。

北京大學的研究說明，就目前而言，中國大多數中產階級似乎在大多數情況下安於現狀。就算考慮到很多中國人可能不願意批評政府，儘管是在調查里，也沒有依據表明較富裕的城市居民有意挑戰黨的統治。

研究發現，自認為屬於社會「中上層」的應答者當中，約60%對當地政府的表現持正面看法。相比之下，自認為屬於最底層級的人當中，這一數據則為48%。

「與工人階層特別是國有部門工人階層相比，我國中產階層的貧富差距感知、幹部信任水平和政府績效評價相對積極，」文中指出。「中產階層具有成為『社會穩定器』的潛質。」

但這也有可能發生變化。中國社會科學院發佈的覆蓋逾3000人的另一項調查發現，中國中產階級要比社會其他成員更積極地參與政治事務。

此項調查自2014年底開始進行了12個月，結果發表在社科院的2016年《社會藍皮書》上。調查發現，北京、上海和廣州的中產階級應答者當中，42.%的人表示，會與身邊人討論政治。只有27.7%的非中產階級成員做出同樣表示。

## 2024年中国国民经济运行统计数据（国家统计局发布，2025年1月17日）

这份文件是国家统计局于2025年1月17日发布的2024年中国全年国民经济运行数据报告，全面涵盖GDP、农业、工业、服务业、消费、投资、外贸、物价、就业、收入及人口等主要经济指标。

### 核心宏观数据
- **GDP**：全年国内生产总值134.9万亿元（1349084亿元），按不变价格计算比上年增长5.0%。分季度看：一季度增长5.3%、二季度4.7%、三季度4.6%、四季度5.4%；四季度环比增长1.6%。分产业：第一产业增加值9.14万亿元（+3.5%）、第二产业49.21万亿元（+5.3%）、第三产业76.56万亿元（+5.0%）。
- 2024年主要发展目标顺利实现，经济运行总体平稳、稳中有进，一揽子增量政策推动经济明显回升。

### 分领域关键数据
1. **农业**：粮食总产量70650万吨（+1.6%）；夏粮14989万吨（+2.6%）、早稻2817万吨（-0.6%）、秋粮52843万吨（+1.4%）；猪牛羊禽肉产量9663万吨（+0.2%），猪肉5706万吨（-1.5%）；生猪出栏70256万头（-3.3%）、年末存栏42743万头（-1.6%）。
2. **工业**：规模以上工业增加值全年增长5.8%（12月增长6.2%）；装备制造业增长7.7%、高技术制造业增长8.9%；新能源汽车产量增长38.7%、集成电路增长22.2%、工业机器人增长14.2%；1-11月规上工业企业利润总额66675亿元（-4.7%）。
3. **服务业**：全年服务业增加值增长5.0%；信息传输/软件/信息技术服务业增长10.9%、租赁和商务服务业增长10.4%。
4. **消费**：社会消费品零售总额487895亿元（+3.5%）；网上零售额155225亿元（+7.2%），实物商品网上零售额130816亿元（+6.5%），占社零总额26.8%；餐饮收入55718亿元（+5.3%）；服务零售额增长6.2%。
5. **投资**：固定资产投资（不含农户）514374亿元（+3.2%）；扣除房地产投资后增长7.2%；基础设施投资+4.4%、制造业投资+9.2%、房地产开发投资-10.6%；民间投资-0.1%（扣除房地产后+6.0%）；高技术产业投资+8.0%。
6. **房地产**：新建商品房销售面积97385万平方米（-12.9%）、销售额96750亿元（-17.1%）；房屋新开工面积-23.0%、竣工面积-27.7%；商品房待售面积75327万平方米（+10.6%）。
7. **外贸**：货物进出口总额438468亿元（+5.0%）；出口254545亿元（+7.1%）、进口183923亿元（+2.3%）；对"一带一路"国家进出口增长6.4%，占比50.3%；机电产品出口占59.4%。
8. **物价**：CPI全年上涨0.2%；核心CPI上涨0.5%；PPI和工业生产者购进价格均下降2.2%；12月CPI同比上涨0.1%。
9. **就业**：全国城镇调查失业率平均值5.1%（同比下降0.1个百分点）；农民工总量29973万人（+0.7%）。
10. **居民收入**：全国居民人均可支配收入41314元（名义+5.3%，实际+5.1%）；城镇居民54188元（实际+4.4%）、农村居民23119元（实际+6.3%）；人均消费支出28227元（实际+5.1%）；恩格尔系数29.8%；人均服务性消费支出占比46.1%。
11. **人口**：年末全国人口140828万人（减少139万人）；出生人口954万人（出生率6.77‰）、死亡人口1093万人（死亡率7.76‰）；人口自然增长率-0.99‰；城镇化率67.00%（提高0.84个百分点）；60岁及以上人口31031万人占22.0%。

### 报告结论与展望
报告指出，2024年经济运行总体平稳、稳中有进，高质量发展取得新进展，主要目标任务顺利完成。同时承认外部环境变化影响加深、国内需求不足、部分企业生产经营困难。下阶段将深化改革开放，实施更加积极有为的宏观政策，扩大国内需求，推动经济持续回升向好。

It analyzes China's household balance sheet (居民资产负债表) — its past, present, and future — drawing comparisons with the US and Japan to forecast changes during the "15th Five-Year Plan" (十五五) period.

**Section 1: Review of China's household balance sheet changes (2017-2023)**

Asset side:
- 2022: Non-financial assets (primarily housing, over 90%) made up 50.8% of household total assets, up 8.4 percentage points from 2017, driven by rapid urbanization and rising housing prices.
- 2023: Household financial assets totaled approximately ¥255.2 trillion. Deposits and cash rose from 56.4% (2017) to 62.0% (2023) of financial assets. Insurance stayed stable at 11-13%; stocks fluctuated between 9.0% and 13.4%, correlated with equity market returns. Other allocations in 2023: insurance 12.2%, stocks 9.4%, securities investment funds 3.4%, bonds 0.5%, and other financial assets (wealth management, trusts) ~31.9 trillion yuan (~12.5%).

Liability side:
- End of 2023: total household liabilities ~¥90.1 trillion, of which loans ~¥88.3 trillion. Personal housing loans fell from 54.1% (2017) to 47.7% of total household loans; consumer loans (ex-housing) ~24.7%; other loans ~27.7%. Housing loan growth correlates with housing prices; consumer loans correlate with income confidence.
- Household leverage (financial liabilities/financial assets) rose then fell, reaching 35.3% in 2023, down 2.6 percentage points from its peak.

**Section 2: International experience**

US (from 1980, matching China's current per-capita GDP ~$13,000):
- End of 2024: total household assets $190.2 trillion (financial 67.8%, non-financial 32.2%). Financial assets: stocks 41.3%, pensions 25.0%, funds 13.2%, currency/deposits 11.5%, bonds 4.8%, insurance 3.0%. Real estate comprised 85.1% of non-financial assets.
- Financial asset share rose from 62.3% (1980) to 67.8% (2024). Mortgage loans stable at 65-76% of household loans; consumer loans 20-30%.

Japan (from 1985, matching China's current per-capita GDP):
- End of 2023: total household assets ¥3350.3 trillion (financial 63.6%, non-financial 36.4%). Financial assets: currency/deposits >50%, stocks 13.7%, insurance 12.9%, pensions 11.9%, funds 5.5%, bonds 1.3%. Land comprised 63.1% of non-financial assets.
- Financial asset share rose from 44.2% (1994) to 63.6% (2023). Pensions rose from 2.3% (1985) to 16.0% (2008) then fell to 11.9% (2023). Housing loans rose from 23.7% (1985) to 56.3% (2023) of loans; consumer loans ~14.3%.

**Section 3: Outlook for China's household balance sheet**

1. **Leverage ratio likely to decline**: China's financial liabilities/financial assets ratio (36.7% average, 2017-2023) is significantly higher than the US (21.8%) and Japan (25.2%). With real estate market changes and population aging, household loan growth may stay low while financial asset growth outpaces liabilities, challenging financial institutions' asset deployment.

2. **Financial assets share likely to rise**: China's 49.2% financial asset share is below US (60%+) and Japan (63.6%). New urban housing demand expected to fall 27-39% during 2026-2030 (to 6.6-8.3 billion sqm/year), reducing non-financial asset share. Secondary (second-hand) home transactions are expected to rise — currently only 38.8% (2023) and 42.4% (2024) of total transactions, versus 80%+ in the US and 67.8% in Japan's major urban areas.

3. **Currency/deposits to remain high; pensions to rise**: China's stock+fund allocation (12.8%) is similar to Japan's (10-20%), suggesting similar risk appetite. Money/deposits likely to stay elevated. Insurance is only 12.2% of financial assets, and pension pillars/GDP is below US and Japan. The personal pension system expanded nationwide in December 2024 (announced by five ministries), creating room for pension asset growth.

4. **Housing loans remain the main loan component**: Even in mature markets, mortgages exceed 55% of household loans (US >60% since 1980; Japan 56.3% in 2023). China's share is 45.5% (down 9.1 points from peak), but international experience suggests it will remain the largest category.

5. **Consumer loans have limited room to grow**: China's consumer credit share (24.7%) roughly matches the US in 1980 (25.5%); Japan peaked below 20%; US ranged 20-30%. Consumer credit correlates with employment. A March 2025 State Council plan aims to boost employment for key groups (graduates, migrant workers, veterans), which could support consumer credit growth.

## World Bank China Economic Update – December 2025

### Overview
This is the World Bank's December 2025 China Economic Update, covering recent economic developments (Q3 2025), the outlook and policy considerations, and a special topic on household savings and financial intermediation in China.

### Recent Economic Conditions (Q3 2025)
- **Growth**: Real GDP grew 1.1% quarter-on-quarter (seasonally adjusted) in Q3, up from 1.0% in Q2, bringing year-to-date growth to 5.2%. Growth was supported by resilient exports despite weakening domestic demand.
- **Consumption**: Final consumption contributed 2.7 percentage points (56.7%) to year-on-year GDP growth in Q3. Retail sales grew only 0.06% month-on-month on average from July to October (seasonally adjusted), down from 0.2% in Q2, as consumer goods subsidy effects faded. Weak labor markets and housing wealth effects kept consumption cautious.
- **Real Estate**: The sector weakened again in Q3. New home sales in 70 cities were down 53% from the 2021 peak as of October. New home prices fell 11.9% and second-hand prices fell 20.2% from July 2021 peaks. Price-to-income ratios remain high relative to other Asian economies, suggesting further adjustment room.
- **Trade**: Goods exports grew 4.7% year-on-year (July–October), driven by demand from developing countries (ASEAN +16%, Africa +33%), offsetting a 27% decline in exports to the US. Imports grew 3.5% (July–October), reversing Q2's 2.7% decline, driven by industrial metals (copper, aluminum, steel) and AI-related tech demand. The average monthly trade surplus narrowed to US$95 billion.
- **External accounts**: The current account surplus rose to an estimated 3.5% of GDP in the first three quarters of 2025 (vs. 2.2% in 2024), offset by capital outflows driven by Chinese investors' portfolio diversification and foreign investors reducing China bond holdings.
- **Inflation**: CPI fell 0.1% year-on-year in the first 10 months of 2025 (vs. +0.2% in 2024), with core inflation at 0.7%, well below the 2% target. PPI fell 2.8% year-on-year over the same period, marking over three consecutive years of producer price deflation, though government-guided capacity reductions moderated deflation in some upstream sectors.
- **Fiscal**: Broad fiscal revenue grew only 0.2% year-on-year in 2025. Land-use-right transfer revenue fell 7.4% in the first ten months. Broad fiscal expenditure grew 3.5% (excluding the one-time central government capital injection to state banks). Local government on-budget debt reached 38% of GDP (up 15+ percentage points since 2020). The broad fiscal deficit widened to 6.1% of GDP from 5.3% a year earlier. In October, the Ministry of Finance announced an additional RMB 500 billion (0.5% of GDP) in local government bond quota for Q4.
- **Monetary and credit**: Net PBC liquidity injection reached 3.3% of GDP in the first three quarters. The 1-year and 5-year LPR rates stayed at 3.0% and 3.5% in Q3. Non-financial sector credit grew 8.7% year-on-year (July–October), with nearly half from government bond issuance. Bank loan growth slowed to 6.4%. The banking system's net interest margin fell to 1.42% in September (down 11 basis points year-on-year). NPL ratio declined 4 basis points to 1.52% by end-September, with provisioning coverage at 207%. Capital adequacy ratio remained stable at 15.4%.
- **Equity markets**: CSI 300 rose 21.2% and HSCEI rose 26.7% from January to October 2025, driven by tech stocks.

### Local Government Debt and Regional Disparities (Box 1)
- Government direct debt reached 61% of GDP in 2024, growing at 14% CAGR since 2015. Local government direct debt is 35% of GDP (58% of total). LGFV debt is estimated at 46% of GDP in 2024.
- Debt accumulation is concentrated in poorer northern and western provinces. Twelve debt-high-risk regions identified in 2023 (Inner Mongolia exited the list in July 2025). Some provinces now spend over 10% of fiscal revenue on interest payments.
- A RMB 10 trillion debt swap program launched in 2024 converted off-budget debt into lower-cost on-budget debt, improving transparency but not necessarily reducing overall debt burdens. Further measures may be needed, including restructuring unsustainable debt and expanding local revenue sources.

### Outlook and Projections
- **2025 GDP growth forecast: 4.9%**; **2026: 4.4%**; 2027: 4.2%.
- CPI forecast: 0.3% (2025), 1.0% (2026), 1.5% (2027).
- Current account: 2.5% of GDP (2025), 1.3% (2026), 0.3% (2027).
- Broad fiscal balance: -8.2% of GDP (2025), -7.7% (2026), -7.0% (2027).
- Government debt: 70.8% of GDP (2025), 77.7% (2026), 82.2% (2027).
- Poverty (using $8.30/day 2021 PPP line): ~15.2% of population (214 million people) below this level in 2024; annual poverty reduction expected to slow from 29 million (2024) to 27 million (2025), 22 million (2026), and 20 million (2027).
- Risks are broadly balanced: downside risks include further real estate weakness and corporate investment delays; upside risks include higher-than-expected fiscal spending and more decisive property stabilization measures.

### Policy Recommendations
Four priority reform areas to boost domestic demand:
1. **Improve social protection** to reduce precautionary savings (unemployment insurance covers only 47% of urban employees; rural migrant and informal workers receive only RMB 223/month in pensions, ~12% of rural per capita income vs. 41% replacement rate for urban formal workers).
2. **Strengthen local fiscal sustainability** by increasing general transfers, implementing the planned consumption tax shift, and considering a recurring property tax.
3. **Improve the business environment** (China's licensing times compare favorably: 6 days for business licenses vs. 28-day emerging market average; 42 days for building permits vs. 56; 6 days for electricity vs. 49), ensuring consistent implementation and limiting discretionary distortions.
4. **Stabilize the real estate market** through market-based price adjustments, improved bankruptcy frameworks, debt restructuring for viable developers, and accelerated asset disposal through AMCs.

The upcoming 15th Five-Year Plan (to be released March 2026) provides an opportunity to integrate these reforms into a unified high-quality development agenda.

### Special Topic: Household Savings and Financial Intermediation
- **High savings rates**: China's gross domestic savings reached 43% of GDP in 2023, well above global and EMDE averages. Household savings represent about half of total domestic savings. Household savings rate was 31.3% of disposable income in 2023, far above the OECD average of 5.4%.
- **Drivers**: Rapid aging, inadequate social security coverage, income inequality, weak labor markets, falling house prices, and limited long-term financial products.
- **Household balance sheet (2022)**: Housing accounts for 47% of household assets; bank deposits 23%; stocks and investment funds 15.4%; bonds 4.3%; insurance 4.8%.
- **Deposits**: Household deposits reached ~RMB 165 trillion (122% of GDP) by September 2025 — 5 times personal mortgage loans and 2 times total retail loans. Real deposit rates have been very low or negative.
- **Financial structure**: Banks hold three-quarters of financial assets, providing cheap funding but potentially weakening price signals and contributing to capital misallocation (rising capital-output ratio, declining marginal returns to capital).
- **Behavioral anomaly**: Despite low real returns, households continue increasing savings (target savings hypothesis). PBC surveys show 63.8% (Q2 2025) and 62.3% (Q3 2025) of urban depositors prefer more savings over spending or investing.
- **Policy priorities for financial rebalancing**:
  1. Diversify household savings options (personal pension accounts — only 60 million participants by 2024; life insurance penetration ~3% vs. 4.5% peers; deepen capital markets, improve pricing mechanisms, tax incentives for long-term savings).
  2. Expand responsible consumer credit through digital innovation (BNPL integrated into Alipay, WeChat Pay, JD; AI-driven credit assessment like Ant Group's "310" model).
  3. Optimize resource allocation through full interest rate liberalization and improved bank governance.
  4. Manage policy trade-offs (expanding credit may raise household debt; rate liberalization may raise borrowing costs and bank funding costs; capital market expansion increases volatility exposure).
</summary>

This Reuters article (published April 24, 2020) reports on a survey by the People's Bank of China (PBOC) regarding the asset and liability structure of urban households in China. The survey, conducted by the PBOC's Department of Survey and Statistics research group and published in the journal "China Finance," covered more than 30,000 urban households across 30 provinces in mid-to-late October 2019, making it one of the most complete and detailed surveys of urban household assets and liabilities ever conducted in China.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Baidu Baike (Wikipedia-like encyclopedia) entry on "中国家庭平均资产" (China's Average Household Assets), providing survey data and analysis on Chinese household wealth based on research from the China Household Finance Survey and Research Center at Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (西南财经大学中国家庭金融调查与研究中心).

Key findings presented in the article include:

1. **Overall Growth**: In 2015, the average Chinese household assets grew 20.2% compared to 2013. The household average assets reached approximately 920,000 RMB (92万), with a video on the page citing household average assets of 3.179 million RMB (317.9万) in a separate context.

2. **Housing Dominance**: Real estate accounted for 69.2% of total household assets in 2015 — more than double the proportion in the United States. This reflects weak asset liquidity, traditional beliefs about homeownership, and relatively low incomes limiting allocation to financial assets.

3. **Financial Asset Growth**: Financial assets saw the largest increase at 59.4%. Stocks grew 92.5% and financial wealth-management products surged 198.5% compared to 2013. However, this growth was deemed "unsustainable" as it relied on volatile financial assets and property. Fixed-term and demand deposits together accounted for 36.3% and 34.4% of savings respectively (over 70% combined), indicating limited financial literacy.

4. **Middle-Income Households**: China had 217 million (2.17亿) middle-income household adults with average wealth of $127,000 USD (approximately 810,000 RMB), ranking first globally in both scale and total wealth. However, middle-income households comprised only 21.4% of the adult population in China compared to nearly 60% in Japan. The article notes China's wealth distribution is "pyramid-shaped" while Japan's is a stable "olive shape."

5. **Financial Literacy Gap**: China's household financial knowledge index was only 42, compared to 75.3 for the US and 78.8 for the Netherlands. Chinese households have lower participation in financial markets due to lack of knowledge and various barriers to bank loans.

6. **Survey Methodology**: The China Household Finance Survey and Research Center conducted nationwide surveys in 2011, 2013, and 2015. The 2015 survey involved 2,500 students from Southwestern University of Finance and Economics and 55 other universities, covering over 40,000 households across 363 districts/counties in 29 provinces, municipalities, and autonomous regions.

The findings were presented by Associate Professor 李凤 (Li Feng), Chief Researcher of the Family Finance Research Department at the center, during the 2015 Korea-Sichuan Province Western Forum. Key recommendations include using government transfer payments to support low-income groups to grow the middle-income population.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: 人民币存款余额_百度百科 ---
URL: https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E4%BA%BA%E6%B0%91%E5%B8%81%E5%AD%98%E6%AC%BE%E4%BD%99%E9%A2%9D/12803659

SUMMARY:
<summary>
人民币存款余额是百度百科上的一篇经济指标词条，定义指银行和其他金融机构在截止到某一时点的以人民币计价的存储金额总和，是反映货币供应量、金融市场流动性以及居民和企业资金储备情况的重要经济指标。该指标统计范围包括活期存款、定期存款和通知存款，一般按月统计。

【发展历程与关键数据】
- 人民币存款余额从1952年的656万元增长至2021年的238.39万亿元
- 2023年末：284.3万亿元，增加25.7万亿元
- 2024年末：302.25万亿元，同比增长6.3%，全年增加17.99万亿元
- 2025年9月末：324.94万亿元，同比增长8%
- 2025年末：328.64万亿元，同比增长8.7%，全年增加26.41万亿元（其中住户存款增加14.64万亿元、非金融企业存款增加2.31万亿元、财政性存款增加6579亿元、非银行业金融机构存款增加6.41万亿元）
- 截至2026年3月末，北京市人民币各项存款余额达30.9万亿元，成为国内首个存款规模突破30万亿元的城市

【基本特征】
- 由住户存款、非金融企业存款、财政性存款、非银行业金融机构存款构成
- 2024年3月末约296万亿元存款总盘子中，居民、企业、政府存款占比分别为49%、27%、14%
- 住户存款从2016年的59.8万亿元增长到2023年的137万亿元，增长超过一倍；非金融企业存款从50万亿元增长到78.8万亿元（增幅57.6%）
- 存款定期化趋势加剧，定期与活期存款比重已由2017年"六四开"升至2024年"七三开"
- 2026年四大行长期定期存款到期规模预计20.37万亿元，以四大行约占全国存款总量40%推算，全国长期定期存款到期规模将达50.93万亿元，存款结构改善有助于缓解商业银行净息差压力

【应用与影响】
- 人民币存款余额是构成广义货币(M2)的重要组成部分，是分析货币总量、评估货币政策效果的关键依据
- 存款增长是支撑广义货币(M2)增长的主要因素
- 存款定期化加剧反映出居民消费有待恢复、总需求不足，存款主要留存在居民部门

【相关研究】
- 2021年末住户存款102.5万亿元，按14亿人口计算人均存款约7.32万元
- 离岸市场人民币存款余额是衡量人民币国际化程度的重要指标，基于2011-2018年香港数据的实证研究表明，人民币汇率预期、跨境汇率差套利及进出口贸易是影响离岸市场人民币存款余额变动的主要原因

【概念区分】
- 人民币存款余额是大范围概念，居民储蓄存款余额是小范围概念（仅包括城乡居民存入银行及农村信用社的储蓄时点数）
</summary>

This webpage presents the full text of the "2023 China Private Wealth Report" (中国私人财富报告 2023), jointly published by China Merchants Bank (招商银行) and Bain & Company (贝恩公司). It is the eighth edition of this series, first launched in 2009, tracking China's private wealth market and high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs). The report is based on over 4,000 survey questionnaires and in-depth interviews with HNW clients across nearly 20 cities (including Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Hangzhou, Nanjing, Wuhan, Chongqing, Xi'an, Qingdao, Shenyang, Xiamen, Hong Kong, Changzhou, Shaoxing, Tangshan, and Hohhot).

KEY MARKET DATA:
- In 2022, China's total personal investable assets reached 278 trillion RMB (2020-2022 CAGR of 7%), projected to exceed 300 trillion RMB by end of 2024.
- In 2022, there were 3.16 million HNWIs (investable assets over 10 million RMB), holding 101 trillion RMB in investable assets (2020-2022 CAGR of 10% for population, 9% for wealth). Average per capita investable assets: ~31.83 million RMB.
- HNW population and wealth expected to grow at ~11% and ~12% CAGR over the next two years.
- Regional distribution: 26 provinces had over 20,000 HNWIs by 2022. Nine provinces exceeded 100,000 (Guangdong, Shanghai, Beijing, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Shandong, Sichuan, Fujian, Hubei). The three major economic circles (Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei, Yangtze River Delta, Pearl River Delta) maintained growth; western regions like Chengdu-Chongqing improved notably. Top five provinces (Guangdong, Shanghai, Beijing, Jiangsu, Zhejiang) held ~44% of HNW population and ~60% of HNW wealth.

MACROECONOMIC CONTEXT:
- China's GDP grew 8.4% in 2021, 3.0% in 2022 (exceeding 120 trillion RMB), and Q1 2023 GDP grew 4.5%, Q2 grew 6.3% as the economy entered recovery.
- 2020-2022: cash and deposits CAGR of 11% (near 5-year high due to precautionary savings); real estate investment cooled (CAGR dropped from 14% to 3%); stock market volatile (SSE index fell 15.1% in 2022); bank wealth management products shrank to 27.7 trillion RMB by end-2022 (net-value products now 95.5% of market); insurance grew modestly.
- Outlook: cash/deposits growth to slow to 9-11%; insurance growth to recover to 9-11%; capital market products and insurance expected to grow at 12% and 10% CAGR respectively.

WEALTH GOALS AND "PERSON-FAMILY-BUSINESS-SOCIETY" NEEDS:
- HNWIs' top wealth goal shifted toward "ensuring wealth security" (top priority), with increased emphasis on personal career/business development and charity/social responsibility; "creating more wealth" declined.
- Nearly 90% of respondents maintain moderate or low risk appetite currently; however, the share willing to try high-return/high-risk investments rose 10 percentage points to 22% (a record high) for the next two years.
- ~60% of domestic investable assets are allocated to cash (28%) and fixed income (27%). Future plans include increasing insurance allocation (especially long-term whole life and annuity products), gold/other alternative assets, and private securities investment, while reducing investment real estate.
- Nearly 70% of respondents plan to increase allocation to emerging assets (e.g., STAR Market/Beijing Stock Exchange equities, REITs, digital assets).
- HNW client structure evolving: new economy group share declined (internet sector volatility), professionals rose, and under-40 clients now represent 49% of respondents (up from 42% in 2021).
- Family needs: 73% have begun wealth succession planning; current methods primarily insurance purchase for children (63%) and property purchase (54%), with family trusts (34%) and corporate equity arrangements (30%) planned for future. Over 70% involved in wealth succession; nearly half considering family trusts. Children's education ranked as second-highest family need.
- Enterprise needs: focused on corporate loans/financing; needs for asset planning, global financing arrangements, listing support, and equity structure optimization noted.
- Social needs: ~40% seek charity donation platforms/project recommendations (43%) and charity structure design (39%, e.g., charitable foundations and charitable trusts). Preferred charitable areas: education equality support (53%), poverty alleviation (43%), elderly/orphan care (41%), rare disease medical aid (37%).

CUSTOMER SEGMENTATION (Chapter 3):
- Segment differences in risk appetite and needs are increasingly pronounced: professionals and professional managers have higher risk appetite; family operators are most conservative.
- Young generation (under 40): higher risk appetite (15% prefer high-return/high-risk vs 10% for older), focused on creating more wealth (48% vs 39%), 62% work in new economy sectors, 94% have bachelor's degree or higher, higher acceptance of emerging assets (46% considering new market equity investments like STAR/Beijing Stock Exchange, REITs 23%, digital transaction assets 23%, structured derivatives 20%), and prefer digital interaction channels. Among family second-generation clients, nearly 60% have wealth inheritance needs and ~45% plan to inherit family business.

CLIENT JOURNEY AND EXPERIENCE (Chapter 4):
- First time introducing the "customer journey" concept with eight key stages: acquisition, account opening, learning about products/services, comprehensive needs communication, obtaining asset allocation/investment advice, investment trading, asset performance tracking and adjustment, and problem resolution.
- Account opening, product/service understanding, and asset performance tracking/adjustment are "detractor-creating" scenarios requiring baseline service standards; comprehensive needs communication, asset allocation advice, and problem resolution are "recommender-creating" scenarios where differentiation creates value.
- High-net-worth clients show high digital acceptance: 40-50% prefer digital-led interaction in early journey stages, but 40-50% prefer human-led service for complex/key stages (needs communication, advice, problem resolution).
- Wealth management institutions should embrace large language models (LLMs like ChatGPT) in digital capability building to support client managers.

COMPETITIVE LANDSCAPE (Chapter 5):
- Key selection criteria for choosing a wealth management institution: professional competence (investment advisor background 63%, client manager market responsiveness 39%) and product capability (stable returns 26%, product range diversity 25%, exclusivity/innovation 10%), plus brand reputation (48%).
- Chinese banks remain the top choice (77% of HNW financial asset allocation in 2023, down from 88% in 2019); securities firms grew to 5% (leveraging equity research capability); insurers reached 3% (positioning on long-term allocation, retirement, and succession needs); foreign private banks held 4-5%.
- Acquisition channels vary by institution type: state-owned banks rely on branch referrals (54%); joint-stock banks on branch referrals (49%) plus friend/family recommendations (22%); securities firms heavily on referrals (40%); foreign banks on brand-driven proactive inquiries (13%) and referrals (~30%).

METHODOLOGY (Appendix):
- Uses Bain's "HNWI Income-Wealth Distribution Model" (top-down approach) with Lorenz curve analysis benchmarked against the US, UK, Japan, and South Korea, plus China Merchants Bank's regional client asset data.
- Survey covered 92 major cities across all key economic regions; interviews conducted in nearly 20 cities; all interviewees had investable assets of at least 10 million RMB.

- Liu Lei (刘磊), Secretary-General of the NIFD National Balance Sheet Research Center, stated that if prices recover moderately and nominal GDP growth stabilizes in 2026, the pressure of passive leverage increases could ease significantly, with the overall trend likely being "stabilization at high levels with structural adjustment" rather than continued rapid increases.
- Ming Ming (明明), Chief Economist at CITIC Securities, expects the macro leverage ratio to remain stable in 2026, with policies focusing on boosting nominal economic growth, optimizing financing structure, "investing in people," and stabilizing households through income and housing price stability.
- The report recommends: accelerating urban-rural income growth plans; city-specific policies to control supply and clear inventory in housing; stabilizing SOE leverage while supporting private enterprise deleveraging (including special relending for clearing arrears); government continuing to increase leverage to "invest in people" through areas like pensions, childcare, education, healthcare, and affordable housing; and mortgage interest subsidies (with a 1% subsidy on the 37.4 trillion yuan mortgage balance reducing interest burden by 374.4 billion yuan, potentially adding 250.68 billion yuan in consumption and boosting retail sales growth by 0.5pp).
- International comparison: BIS data shows developed economies and emerging markets had macro leverage ratios of 268.1% and 223.1% respectively as of end-Q2 2025, with China at a relatively high level.

The article was published on January 28, 2026, by author Du Chuan (杜川).

**Key Rankings (end-2024, among 40+ countries in BIS data):**

**Three versions of China's macro leverage ratio:** BIS, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), and PBoC versions exist. The CASS and PBoC versions count only central government bonds and local government bonds as government debt (82 trillion yuan at end-2024), while BIS also includes some local government financing platform (LGFV) debt in government debt (37 trillion yuan difference). The PBoC version shows the highest macro leverage ratio, with household leverage already exceeding developed economies.

- China's corporate leverage 138.1% (end-2024), peaked at 148.6% in 2015, ranked 6th globally

**Government sector:**
- China's government leverage 88.4% (end-2024), ranked 12th; even at the highest BIS version, still below developed economies
